Improved methane production of corn straw by the stimulation of calcium
peroxide
Shan-Fei Fua,b,c, Kai-Qiang Chena,b, Wen-Xin Suna,b, Rong Zhua,b,c, Yi Zhengd, Hua Zoua,b,c,⁎
a School of Environment and Civil Engineering, Jiangnan University, Wuxi, Jiangsu Province 214122, PR China
b Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Anaerobic Biotechnology, Jiangnan University, Wuxi, Jiangsu Province 214122, PR China
c Jiangsu Collaborative Innovation Center of Technology and Material of Water Treatment, Suzhou 215009, PR China
d Department of Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, Clemson University, 342 Computer Court, Anderson, SC 29625, USA
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Calcium peroxide
Hydrolysis
Micro-aeration
Microbial community structure
A B S T R A C T
This research focused on the eﬀect of calcium peroxide (CaO2) addition on anaerobic digestion (AD) of corn
straw. It was found that the CaO2 dose of 0.032–0.256 g·g−1 TVS (total VS of substrate and inoculum) had
positive eﬀect on the AD of corn straw by improving methane yield and content in biogas. Maximum methane
yield was achieved at the CaO2 dose of 0.032 g·g−1 TVS, which was 241.6 mL·g−1 VSS (VS of substrate) and 11%
higher than that of the control. Methane content in biogas also increased according to the in situ immobilization
of CO2 by Ca(OH)2 that produced via the reaction of CaO2 with water (XRD analysis results). Microbial com-
munity structure was signiﬁcantly aﬀected by CaO2 addition. The variation of bacterial community structure led
to higher hydrolysis rate, and the variation of archaea community structure ensured the proceeding of metha-
nogenesis process. The use of CaO2 could be a cost-eﬀective method to improve methane production of corn
straw because it avoids harsh condition and high cost (e.g., chemical and energy inputs) associated with con-
ventional chemical treatment techniques. The digestate from the AD with the addition of CaO2 can contain high
CaCO3 content, making it a potential soil amendment for acidic soil.
1. Introduction
Using cellulosic biomass as renewable resource to produce bioe-
nergy has attracted global interests during the past decades [1,2].
Anaerobic digestion (AD) technology has been widely used for organic
waste disposal and energy production [3]. In AD process, the cellulosic
biomass can be converted into biogas, a mixture of methane, carbon
dioxide and small amounts of other gases [4,5]. Biogas typically has a
caloriﬁc value of 22,000–25,000 kJ·m−3 [6], therefore it is considered
as one of the major renewable energy source. In general, AD process can
be divided into four stages: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, and
methanogenesis [7]. Cellulosic biomass is mainly composed of cellu-
lose, hemicellulose and lignin, and they bind with each other tightly by
non-covalent forces and covalent cross-linkage [8]. Due to the complex
components and strong structure of cellulosic biomass, the hydrolysis
was demonstrated to be the rate-limiting step of AD [9,10], resulting in
some common issues such as long retention time and low eﬃciency.
Substrate pretreatment is the most studied method to improve the hy-
drolysis rate [7,10], including chemical, thermal, mechanical, and
biological pretreatment as well as their combination. During pretreat-
ment, the structure of substrate is partly destroyed. Which makes the
substrate more accessible to microorganisms and extracellular hydro-
lytic enzymes present in AD. However, the pretreatment process is
usually conducted in a separate reactor with the input of additional
energy and/or chemicals, which leads to increased cost. Especially, the
chemical pretreatment might also cause environmental problems. As a
result, an economically feasible and environmentally friendly method
should be developed to improve the hydrolysis rate and the overall AD
eﬃciency of cellulosic substrate.
Recent research has shown the hydrolysis stage of AD could be
accelerated under microaerobic condition [11,12]. In addition, micro-
aerobic treatment (microaerobic pretreatment or introduction of lim-
ited oxygen into the AD system) has been successfully applied to im-
prove the methane yield in several studies [13–16]. The microaerobic
condition was considered to support the growth of aerobic and/or fa-
cultative microorganisms, which stimulated the secretion of extra-
cellular hydrolytic enzymes (e.g., cellulose and protease) [14]. The
production of more such enzymes could improve the hydrolysis of
cellulosic substrate and ﬁnally increase the AD eﬃciency. Compared
with other methods, the micro-aeration in AD by using oxygen only
needs limited amount of oxygen or air, which is simpler, cheaper and
more attractive [15].

Calcium peroxide (CaO2), a commonly used oxidant has been ex-
tensively applied in agriculture, aquiculture, environmental restoration,
and pharmaceuticals [17]. It can react with water to produce calcium
hydroxide [Ca(OH)2] and oxygen [17]. Due to this property, CaO2
could be used as an alternative additive to provide oxygen for AD
process and create a microaerobic condition to enhance the hydrolysis
of substrate. Previous studies have demonstrated CaO2 was an eﬃcient
additive for contaminant (e.g., phenolic endocrine disrupting com-
pounds and polychlorinated biphenyls-containing electrical insulating
oil) removal with the action of reactive oxygen species (ROS) derived
from CaO2 [17,18]. In the AD of active sludge, CaO2 was used as an
eﬃcient additive to improve the activities of both hydrolytic enzymes
and acid-forming enzymes, and therefore enhance the hydrolysis and
acidiﬁcation of active sludge [19]. In addition, Ca(OH)2 produced via
the reaction of CaO2 with water could immobilize CO2 in situ (Ca
(OH)2 + CO2 →CaCO3 + H2O), and therefore improve the methane
content in biogas. Also, the produced Ca(OH)2 or CaCO3 could con-
tribute additional alkalinity to the AD system, and therefore beneﬁt the
production of soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) and volatile
fatty acids (VFs) [20]. However, the %OH generation from CaO2 was
found to have signiﬁcant inhibition on methanogens [21]. In the study
of Li et al. [19], the production of methane was inhibited with the CaO2
dose in the range of 0.05–0.3 g·g−1 VSS (volatile suspended solid).
Therefore, the dose of CaO2 needs to be well controlled when it is used
as an additive to enhance the AD eﬃciency. A critical dose should be
determined between the stimulation eﬀect on hydrolysis (due to O2 and
H2O2 generation from CaO2) and the inhibition eﬀect (arising from %OH
generation from CaO2) on methanogenesis. In addition, the critical dose
may vary between cellulosic feedstocks.
As a result, this study explored the possibility of using CaO2 as an
additive to increase the AD eﬃciency of corn straw. The eﬀect of CaO2
addition on the methane yield, methane concentration and SCOD (so-
luble chemical oxygen demand) production were analyzed. The dy-
namics of microbial community structure during the AD process were
also investigated. The implementation of this study would provide a
cost-eﬀective solution to improve the AD performance on cellulosic
feedstocks.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Corn straw was collected from the ﬁeld of PingDu, Qingdao,
Shandong province, China. Before AD, the corn straw was air-dried to
moisture content of 8% and chopped to particle size of about 0.5 cm.
The inoculum used in this study was obtained from a mesophilic AD (at
35 °C) plant which uses cow dung and corn straw as substrates with
hydraulic retention time of 35 days. Before used, the inoculum was
ﬁltered through a sieve with the opening of ten mesh. The character-
istics of substrate and inoculum were shown in Table 1.
2.2. Batch AD test
Mesophilic (37 °C) batch AD of corn straw was conducted in quad-
ruplicate for a total fermentation time of 43 days. To start AD, 5.33 g
(TS) corn straw, 2.67 g (TS) inoculum and diﬀerent amount of CaO2
were mixed in 300-mL glass bottles. The doses of CaO2 were 0 (control),
0.032, 0.064, 0.128, and 0.256 g·g−1 TVS (total VS of substrate and
inoculum), respectively (coded as C0, C1, C2, C3, and C4). A blank
group containing inoculum only (without substrate or CaO2) was also
carried out to test the biogas production from inoculum. The working
volumes for all AD batches were adjusted to 200 mL by adding nutrient
solution as described in Angelidaki et al. [22]. All the bottles were
ﬂushed with N2 for 5 min to remove the oxygen. After sealed with
rubber stoppers, all the bottles were incubated in a shaking water bath
at 37 °C with the shaking speed of 120 rpm.
2.3. Analysis of the fermentation residue by X-ray diﬀraction (XRD)
After AD, the digestates were collected and dried at 105 °C for 8 h
followed by milling. The digestate powders were then subjected to
CaCO3 analysis with a wide angle X-ray diﬀraction (Bruker D8
Advance, Germany) at 40 kV and 40 mA in the scanning angle of 5–80°
(2θ) at a scanning speed of 1.0°/min.
2.4. Analysis of AD performance
Biogas production was monitored in volume with water displace-
ment method, and the methane content in biogas was analyzed with a
gas chromatograph (GC, SP 6890, Shandong Lunan Inc., China) using
argon as carrier gas. The GC was equipped with a Porapak Q stainless
steel analytical column (180 cm long and 3 mm OD) and a thermal
conductivity detector. The analysis temperatures of the injector, de-

Spectrophotometric method was used for SCOD measurement [23].
Prior to the SCOD analysis, AD eﬄuent samples were centrifuged for
5 min at 10,000 rpm and the supernatants were ﬁltered through
0.45 µm glass microﬁber paper [23]. TS and VS of the substrate and
inoculum were measured by following the standard method [24]. The
element contents of corn straw were quantiﬁed with an elemental
analyzer (Vario EL III elemental analyzer).
2.5. Analysis of the microbial community structure
During AD process, aliquots of 8 mL eﬄuent were collected from all
the groups (C0-C4) at the 3rd, 12th and 40th day of AD. As C1 showed
the highest methane production, it was selected as an example from the
treatment groups (C1-C4) to compare with C0 for analyzing the eﬀect of
CaO2 addition on the microbial community structure. The collected
eﬄuent samples were stored in a -80 °C freezer until used. In this study,
genomic DNA was extracted using the E.Z.N.A.® DNA Kit (Omega Bio-
tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.) according to manufacturer’s instruction. One
percent agarose gel electrophoresis and spectrophotometry (optical
density at 260 nm/280 nm ratio) were used to check the quality of
extracted DNA. The V3–V4 hypervariable regions of the 16S rRNA gene
were subjected to high-throughput sequencing which was done by the
Beijing Allwegene Tech, Ltd (Beijing, China) using the Illumina Miseq
PE300 sequencing platform (Illumina, Inc., CA, USA). The V3–V4 re-
gions of the bacterial 16S rRNA gene were ampliﬁed by using the
universal forward primer 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3)
and reverse primer 806R (5′-GACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′).
These primers contained a set of 8-nucleotide barcodes sequence
unique to each sample. The PCR program included steps of 95 °C for
5 min, 25 cycles at 95 °C for 30 s, 55 °C for 30 s, and 72 °C for 30 s as
well as a ﬁnal extension of 72 °C for 10 min. The PCR reactions were
performed in triplicate in 25 μL mixtures containing 2.5 μL of 10X

with the conﬁdence threshold of 90%.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Eﬀect of CaO2 on total gas production and methane content
As shown in Table 2, the addition of CaO2 aﬀected total biogas/
methane yields and methane content diﬀerently. The CaO2 dose of
0.032 g·g−1 TVS (C1) achieved the maximum biogas (476 mL·g−1 VSs)
and methane (241.6 mL·g−1 VSs) yields. Further increase of CaO2 dose
caused signiﬁcant decrease of total biogas yield compared to the control
(C0), especially when CaO2 doses were 0.128 (C3) and 0.256 (C4) g·g−1
TVS. All CaO2 dose levels (C1–C4) achieved higher cumulative methane
yield over C0 while further increase of CaO2 dose from C1 to C4 slightly
reduced the cumulative methane yield. With the addition of CaO2, the
methane content was signiﬁcantly increased from 49.4 to 66.8%, and
higher CaO2 dose resulted in higher methane content, which could be
one of the reasons why groups C3 and C4 still had higher cumulative
methane yield than C0 even though their cumulative biogas yield was
lower. The caloriﬁc value of biogas derived from methane component
in biogas, thus higher methane content can lead to a higher caloriﬁc
value of biogas. Biogas upgrading to increase the methane purity is an
indispensable step prior to its utilization. Therefore, high methane
content in biogas is beneﬁcial for the reduction of energy consumption
and cost for biogas upgrading and its ﬁnal applications.
The microaerobic condition resulted from the presence of CaO2 in
AD could largely contribute to the increased cumulative methane yield.
The added CaO2 can react with water and release oxygen during AD
(2CaO2 + 2H2O →2Ca(OH)2 + O2↑) [18]. The produced oxygen can
induce the growth of facultative bacteria that produced more extra-
cellular enzymes and improved the hydrolysis eﬃciency, leading to
increased methane yield [11,25,26]. The CO2 in the biogas could be
partly immobilized in situ by Ca(OH)2 according to the following re-
action: [Ca(OH)2 + CO2 →CaCO3 + H2O]. Biogas is mainly composed
by methane and carbon dioxide. The methane content in biogas is
calculated according to the following formula: methane content in
biogas = methane/biogas. The produced Ca(OH)2 could partly im-
mobilize carbon dioxide with no eﬀect on methane. The amount of
biogas decreased due to the immobilization of carbon dioxide, however
the amount of methane did not change, which led to increased methane
content in biogas. In addition, the produced Ca(OH)2 and CaCO3 could
improve the acidic buﬀer capacity of the AD system, which could
beneﬁt the production of SCOD and volatile fatty acids (VFAs), and
therefore resulting in higher methane yield and content [20].
In XRD analysis of AD digestates (Fig. 1), it was found that all AD
digestates with the addition of CaO2 (C1-C4) had much stronger CaCO3
peak signals (at 2θ = 29°) than that with no CaO2 addition (C0).
Moreover, the intensity of CaCO3 peaks increased with the increase of
CaO2 dose. These results veriﬁed the fact that the added CaO2 into the

3.2. Eﬀect of CaO2 on daily and cumulative methane yields
As shown in Fig. 2A, the daily methane yields of C0-C2 followed the
same trend with the peak value at the 5th day of AD. However, C1 and
C2 had higher daily methane yield than C0 after the 2nd day of AD,
which may be due to the micro-aeration and/or in situ CO2 im-
mobilization derived from the presence of CaO2. In contrast, the daily
methane yields of C3 and C4 were lower than that of C0 until the 6th
and 10th day of AD, respectively, and their peaks delayed to the 8th and
12th day of AD, respectively. As reported in previous studies, the added
CaO2 could react with water and produced hydroxyl radical (%OH) [21],
which was an inhibitor for methanogens [19]. In this study, the higher
CaO2 doses in C3 and C4 may generate more %OH in AD and inhibited
methane production to certain extent, leading to late occurrence of
peak daily methane yield. Nevertheless, the daily methane yields of C3
and C4 exceeded that of C0 in the late stage of AD, which may indicate
that the beneﬁt of CaOH2 addition overwhelmed its inhibition eﬀect.
The timely cumulative methane yield also reﬂects the beneﬁt of
CaO2 for AD (Fig. 2B), i.e., the ﬁnal total methane yields for all CaO2
treatment groups (C1-C4) are higher than that of the control group (C0)

and rank in the order of C1 > C2 > C3 > C4 with the increase of
CaO2 dose. The maximum ﬁnal methane yield (241.6 mL·g−1 VSs) was
obtained with the CaO2 doses of 0.032 g·g−1 TVS (C1), which was 11%
higher than that of C0. The groups of C1 and C2 had higher cumulative
methane yield than C0 during the whole AD process, and the incre-
ments enlarged with the time. On the contrary, the cumulative methane
yields of C3 and C4 were not always higher than that of C0 until the
11th and 23rd day of AD.
Improved AD performance by the addition of CaO2 could be ex-
plained as follows: (1) added CaO2 could reacted with water and re-
leased O2 [19,27], which supported the growth of facultative/aerobic
bacteria and induced the production of more extracellular enzymes to
increase hydrolysis rate; (2) H2O2/%OH were the intermediates of the
reaction between CaO2 and H2O, and could act on the cellulosic sub-
strate to destroy its structure, making it more accessible to biological
degradation during AD; and (3) the produced Ca(OH)2 and CaCO3 could
contribute to the alkalinity resulting in higher acid buﬀer capacity of
the AD system, which could beneﬁt for the hydrolysis of substrate and
lead to more SCOD and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production, and
therefore provide more available substrate for methane production
[20]. The overdose of CaO2 can inhibit methane production (e.g., C3/
C4 vs C0 in the early stage of AD), which might attribute to the in-
hibition of methanogens by excessive %OH and O2 released from the
reaction of CaO2 with water. According to Fig. 2A/B and Table 1, the
beneﬁts of CaO2 could include both micro-aeration and in situ CO2
immobilization. The signiﬁcance of these two beneﬁts could switch
depending on the dose of CaO2. Therefore, using CaO2 as an additive to
improve the AD performance, the dosage is critical to maximize its
beneﬁts.
3.3. Eﬀect of CaO2 on the SCOD concentration during the AD of corn straw
The overall variations of SCOD concentration in AD process for all
groups (C0-C4) followed the same trend, i.e., initial peaking, gradual
decrease in mid-stage and ﬁnal rapid decrease to a similar value
(Fig. 3). The SCOD concentration showed a dynamic balance between
SCOD production from hydrolysis/acidiﬁcation process and subsequent
consumption by methanogens. As shown in Fig. 3, the addition of CaO2
had signiﬁcant eﬀect on the SCOD concentration during AD, i.e., the
groups (C1–C4) with CaO2 addition generally achieved higher SCOD
concentrations than C0. The highest SCOD concentrations for diﬀerent
groups positively correlated with the CaO2 doses. The maximum SCOD
for C4 was 2575 mg·L−1 (53.7% higher than that of C0). Compared with
C0, C1 and C2 had slightly higher SCOD concentrations and con-
sumption (reﬂected by their similar ﬁnal SCOD concentration) as a
whole, which indicated the higher hydrolysis/acidiﬁcation eﬃciency in
C1 and C2, thus achieving higher daily and cumulative methane yields
as shown in Fig. 2. For C3 and C4, the SCOD accumulation was found at
the initial stage of AD (Fig. 3) due to the inhibition of methanogens,
which reduced methane production (Fig. 2). Afterwards, the produced
SCOD was consumed rapidly (Fig. 3), leading to a higher methane yield
(shown in Fig. 2) probably because the inhibitor %OH was consumed for
CO2 immobilization, simultaneously mitigating the inhibition on me-
thanogens and reducing CO2 content in biogas. Treating waste active
sludge, Li et al. [19] also found the use of CaO2 increased the SCOD
concentration signiﬁcantly during anaerobic fermentation, i.e., 61%
higher SCOD concentration was achieved with the CaO2 dose of
0.3 g·g−1 VSs, compared to the control with no CaO2 addition.
3.4. Analysis of the microbial community structure of AD
The eﬀect of CaO2 on the microbial community structure of AD was
reﬂected by the Shannon diversity index and relative abundance of
sequence at phylum level (Figs. 4 and 5). During AD, the Shannon di-
versity indexes of both C0 and C1 increased with time. The Shannon
diversity indexes of C0 at the 3rd, 12th and 40th day of AD were 3.93,
4.12 and 4.75, respectively, while they were 3.86, 4.60 and 4.70, re-
spectively for C1 (Fig. 4). In comparison, the Shannon diversity indexes
of C0 at the 3rd and 40th day were slightly higher than those of C1,
while the Shannon diversity index of C0 at the 12th day was lower than
that of C1. One of the reasons behind this result may be that the micro-
aeration generated by CaO2 in C1 promoted the growth of aerobic and/
or facultative microorganisms in AD, which led to higher microbial
diversity in C1 at certain stage (e.g., the 12th day in this study) of AD.
Similarly, Lim et al. [28] also reported the microbial diversity under
microaerobic condition was signiﬁcantly higher than that under

As shown in Fig. 5, the microbial community structures of AD
system changed versus time and were signiﬁcantly aﬀected by the ad-
dition of CaO2. During the whole AD process, Bacteroidetes was the most
dominant phylum followed by Firmicutes. Proteobacteria, Euryarchaeota,
Chloroﬂexi, and Synergistetes were also among the dominant phyla. With
the proceeding of AD, the relative abundances of Bacteroidetes and
Proteobacteria decreased, while the relative abundances of Atribacteria,
Cloacimonetes, Spirochaetae, and Lentisphaerae increased. The relative
abundances of Firmicutes in C1 at the 3rd and 12th day of AD were 3.8%
and 39.6% higher than those in C0, respectively. Microorganisms af-
ﬁliating to the phylum Firmicutes were reported to be associated with
the production of extracellular enzymes (e.g., cellulases and proteases),
the degradation of organic compound and the formation of VFAs [29].
Therefore, the higher abundance of Firmicutes in C1 resulted in its
stronger ability than C0 of degrading complex organic compounds. Si-
milar to the results obtained in this study, Li et al. [16] also found that
the relative abundance of Firmicutes increased signiﬁcantly in the pre-
sence of CaO2. Microorganisms belonging to phyla Bacteroidetes and
Proteobacteria were reported to play crucial roles in hydrolysis and
acetogenesis steps of AD [30,31]. Consequently, the higher relative
abundances of Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria in C1 than C0 yielded
higher hydrolysis eﬃciency associated with higher SCOD in C1.
Conventionally, oxygen is considered lethal to methanogenic mi-
croorganisms [32]. However, some studies reported methanogens from
genera Methanobacterium and Methanosarcina showed a certain oxygen
tolerance capability [26,33]. It was found in this study that the relative
abundances of genus Methanobacterium in C1 at the 3rd and 12th day of
AD were much higher than those in C0 (Table S1), leading to higher
methane yield in C1 than C0. Therefore, a certain level of micro-aera-
tion in AD does not impair methanogenesis for methane production.
It appears that the variation of microbial community structure due
to the CaO2 addition is one of the main reasons for the improved AD
performance on corn straw toward higher methane yield. The variation
of bacterial community structure could lead to higher hydrolysis rate,
and the variation of archaea community structure ensured the pro-
ceeding of methanogenesis process.
4. Conclusions
The addition of CaO2 into the AD of corn straw improved the pro-
cess performance signiﬁcantly in increasing SCOD generation, methane
yield and content in biogas as well as the gas production rate. Such
beneﬁts of CaO2 could be resulted from its capabilities of: (i) improving
hydrolysis eﬃciency of cellulosic substrate, (ii) increasing methane
content in biogas by in situ CO2 immobilization and (iii) providing
additional buﬀer capacity for the AD system by contributing alkalinity.
However, %OH derived from the reaction of CaO2 and H2O inhibited
methanogens to some extent. Therefore, the dose of CaO2 needs to be
well balanced between the beneﬁcial and inhibition eﬀect when it is
used as an additive in AD process. In this study, the CaO2 dose of
0.032 g·g−1 TVS achieved the optimum methane yield. The addition of
CaO2 seems to improve the microbial community structure of AD to-
ward beneﬁting its performance. The utilization of CaO2 as an additive
could be a cost-eﬀective technique to enhance the AD of cellulosic
substrates.
